rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to retain early compounds while promoting elution of all 10 compounds within the acquisition window. The retention and resolution pattern will guide subsequent adjustments to gradient range, duration, and temperature.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin survives. Keep temperature and gradient endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient steepness.

Use an intermediate gradient duration to recover separation in the crowded middle region without returning to the long scouting run. This tests whether full resolution can be achieved near the onset of the time penalty.

Test temperature selectivity with a 5 °C decrease while retaining the promising 14-minute gradient. Only one pair remains below baseline resolution, so a modest selectivity shift could achieve full resolution without a time penalty.

The temperature change shifted the crowded middle peaks substantially, suggesting useful selectivity differences. Test the high-temperature limit to seek a better-separated elution order while shortening retention and preserving a zero time penalty.

Back off from 60 °C to improve the newly crowded early-middle pair, and lengthen the gradient slightly to support separation across the middle cluster. The shorter retention at elevated temperature should leave room for this change without a time penalty.

At 55 °C, the middle cluster appears to have changed elution order relative to 40 °C, so a slightly steeper gradient may improve the remaining critical pair. Shortening to 14 minutes tests this while retaining ample separation elsewhere and a zero time penalty.

Shortening the gradient from 16 to 14 minutes improved the only critical pair; another two-minute reduction may lift its resolution above 1.5. The next-tightest pair has some margin at R = 2.18, making this a promising test for the maximum CRF.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the R = 1.59 pair while aiming to keep the other critical pair above 1.5. This tests a neighboring method that may also achieve the maximum CRF with a different balance of resolution margins.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction for an alternative optimum with improved resolution margins. The early peaks have ample separation, allowing this adjustment while monitoring the two critical middle pairs.

Reduce gradient steepness to recover the R = 1.29 pair while retaining the improved separation of the other critical pair at the higher starting organic fraction. This may yield another maximum-score method with better minimum resolution and no time penalty.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek larger resolution margins around the two critical middle pairs. Injection 11 supports this direction; monitor early-peak compression while testing another potential maximum-score method.

Slightly flatten the gradient from injection 12 to improve the R = 1.41 pair, using the other critical pair’s R = 1.74 margin. Last-peak retention should remain below the time-penalty threshold, making this a promising alternative maximum-score method.

Test one further decrease in gradient steepness to improve the R = 1.63 pair while preserving the other critical pair’s margin. This may increase minimum resolution at the already-achieved maximum CRF, provided the last peak remains within the zero-penalty time window.

This gradient slope lies between injections 13 and 14, where the two critical pairs trade resolution margin. Test whether it preserves CRF 1.000 with a better-balanced minimum resolution and slightly earlier last-peak elution than injection 14.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test temperature sensitivity around injection 15, which has the largest observed minimum resolution. A 5 °C decrease will reveal whether this alternative optimum tolerates a temperature change or encounters renewed co-elution.

Test the upper-temperature neighbor of injection 15 to complete the local temperature-sensitivity check. The maximum CRF is already secured, but this run will show whether higher temperature preserves full resolution or creates a different critical pair.

At 60 °C, return to the low starting organic fraction and use a shallower gradient than injection 5 to improve its R = 0.64 pair. This tests for a maximum-score alternative at a different temperature while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Return to 55 °C and test a slightly shallower slope than injection 11, which achieved CRF 1.000. This should improve its tighter early-middle separation while aiming to preserve baseline resolution of the other critical pair and zero time penalty.

Test a gradient slope between injections 13 and 15 to better balance their two critical pairs. This neighboring method may retain the maximum CRF while slightly improving minimum resolution relative to injection 15.

This slope lies between injections 13 and 20 and may balance the two critical resolutions near 1.7. The maximum CRF is already achieved; this tests an alternative with slightly shorter retention than injection 20 and comparable separation margins.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 11 to shorten retention while balancing its two critical pairs near R = 1.6. This seeks a faster alternative with more resolution margin than injection 8, not a score above the already-achieved maximum.

Preserve injection 11’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the programmed gradient earlier. Its last peak eluted before this shortened gradient would end at the outlet, so this method should retain CRF 1.000 with a lower final organic fraction.

Preserve injection 8’s gradient slope and temperature while ending the gradient at a lower organic fraction. Since all peaks previously eluted before the shortened gradient would end at the outlet, this should reproduce the fastest observed maximum-score separation.

Use nearly the same gradient slope as injection 21, which achieved CRF 1.000 with both critical resolutions near 1.70, but end at a lower organic fraction. This should preserve strong separation margins and zero time penalty with a shorter programmed gradient.
